study.title: John 21 The apparition of the Risen One, the Restoration of Peter and the Final Testimony
study.overview: John 21 presents the last manifestation of Jesus to the disciples in the sea of Tiberias, where he transforms a night of fruitless work into abundance, reveals himself as the risen Lord and shares a meal with them. Then Jesus deals directly with Peter's restoration, asking for his love and entrusting him with the care of his flock. The chapter ends with the correction of a misunderstanding about John and a statement about the immeasurable greatness of the works of Jesus, ending the gospel with humility and reverence.

outline.title: Jesus appears in the sea and guides fishing
outline.explanation: The disciples return to fishing, spend the night without result, and by the word of Jesus, the net is filled with fish. The episode shows that the fruit of mission and work depends on the initiative of the Risen Lord.

outline.title: Recognition, provision and communion at the table
outline.explanation: The beloved disciple recognizes Jesus, Peter runs to meet him, and the Lord had already prepared coals, fish and bread. The meal reaffirms the bodily reality of the resurrection and the closeness of Jesus to his own.

outline.title: Restoration of Peter, called to follow-up and final testimony
outline.explanation: Jesus confronts and heals Peter's fall through three questions, entrusts him with the shepherding of his people, announces his future suffering and corrects the curiosity about John. The chapter concludes with the assertion that the written testimony is true and with the idea that the work of Jesus exceeds any complete record.

study.context: The chapter reports that the scene takes place next to the sea of Tiberias, also called the Sea of Galilee in the text itself. The notes indicate that some disciples were fishing, which should not be read as abandonment of the faith, but as a return to an earlier occupation. It is also mentioned that the meal included bread and fish, common elements in the food of that region, and that the fire of coals evokes the denial of Peter in a previous scene.
study.theology: John 21 points out that the risen Christ continues as lord of creation, provision and mission. Milant fishing shows that the success of the disciples' work depends on the word of Jesus, not just human effort. The meal prepared by him reveals pastoral care and restored communion. The dialogue with Peter is especially theological: before entrusting the service, Jesus deals with love, for authentic shepherding is born of a real relationship with Christ. The three questions serve not only to repeat Peter's fall, but to reorient him to repentance, humility and responsibility. The announcement of Peter's type of death links discipleship and fidelity to the end, showing that following Jesus includes suffering. Finally, the closure states that the apostolic witness is true, but also limited before the greatness of Jesus: Scripture is sufficient to lead to faith, even though it does not disgust the person and works of the Lord.

scholarViews.insight: The many other things that Jesus made show that the gospel contains with the awareness that the greatness of Christ surpasses any written account, even though what has been recorded is sufficient and precious.
Jesus appears to the disciples as they fished, not only in solemn meetings; thus, he can make himself known also in the common and daily occupations of his people.
The order to launch the net on the right side of the boat is presented as the means chosen by Christ to work the miracle; the success of fishing depends entirely on the Lord's direction.

questions: What does this scene teach about the dependence on our efforts of Christ's direction, even when we already have experience and skill?
Why does Jesus restore Peter by asking about love before entrusting him pastoral responsibility?
How does Jesus' correction toward John help us to avoid undue comparisons between different callings?
study.practice: This passage invites Christ to recognize Christ in the common tasks, to obey his word before seeking results, and to allow him to treat our faults before sending us to service. It also calls the church to value pastoral care as a fruit of true love for Jesus, not of ambition or comparison. In practice, this means serving with humility, accepting correction, and trusting that the Lord supports both the mission and the personal life of the disciple.
study.uncertainty: The biblical text does not explain in detail why Peter returned to fishing, and the notes only suggest that this does not indicate weakening of faith. There is also no safe base in the notes to go beyond what is said about the exact meaning of fishing for 153 fish, the bonfire or the precise way of Peter's death; therefore, more speculative readings were avoided.
